narrative:
Your application was denied because the model estimated a 68.8% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. In practical terms, it judged failure more likely than success, though not certain; it still implied about a 31% chance of passing.

The strongest driver was your third-year class standing. You were in the third decile, noticeably below the accepted-student average of about the sixth decile, and this pushed the prediction most strongly toward failure. Your first-year standing was the second most influential factor: a fourth decile versus an accepted average near the sixth decile, also pushing toward failure. Your family income bracket—upper-middle—was the third factor and added a smaller push toward failure. Although upper-middle income was common among accepted students, the model treated it as a modest risk factor in your case.

To improve a future application, ask admissions for specific feedback, focus on raising your academic standing in any additional coursework, consider retaking the LSAT if you can meaningfully improve it, and explain any circumstances behind your earlier grades. A concrete bar-preparation plan and evidence of sustained academic improvement would help show that the predicted risk can be reduced.
